reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases / Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
clinicalPearls: Myiasis is infestation of living tissue by dipterous (fly) larvae; clinical patterns include furuncular (boil-like), wound (traumatic), migratory (creeping), and cavity/body-orifice forms
Furuncular myiasis is classically caused by the human botfly (Dermatobia hominis) in the Americas and the tumbu fly (Cordylobia anthropophaga) in sub-Saharan Africa
Dermatobia eggs are carried to skin by biting insects (phoresis), whereas tumbu fly eggs are laid on soil or drying laundry and larvae penetrate contact skin
The typical furuncular lesion is a painful nodule with a central punctum that intermittently discharges serosanguineous fluid; patients often describe movement or a sensation of crawling
A central breathing pore that bubbles, and sometimes a visible larval tip, help confirm the diagnosis; occlusion can bring the larva to the surface
Wound and cavity myiasis (e.g. screwworm) can be aggressively tissue-destructive and occurs in neglected wounds, orifices or debilitated patients
Treatment is removal of the larva (occlusion and extraction or minor surgical removal), wound care, and tetanus/antibiotic cover for secondary infection where indicated
reference.pathophysiology: Fly larvae invade host tissue by species-specific routes: some deposit larvae directly, some lay eggs transferred by biting arthropods, and others deposit eggs on soil or clothing from which larvae penetrate intact or broken skin. The larva develops within the dermis or a wound, feeding on tissue and exudate while maintaining a respiratory opening at the skin surface. Local host inflammation produces a furuncle-like nodule in obligate skin-dwelling species, whereas facultative or obligate wound feeders such as screwworm can burrow and destroy tissue extensively. Secondary bacterial infection frequently complicates the lesion.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination with travel/exposure history and inspection of the central punctum
Occlusion test to observe the larval breathing movements
Dermoscopy or ultrasound to visualise the embedded larva in furuncular myiasis
Identification of the extracted larva to species where relevant
Wound swab and culture if secondary bacterial infection is suspected
redFlags: Aggressive wound or cavity (e.g. nasal, orbital, aural) myiasis with rapid tissue destruction
Screwworm infestation requiring prompt eradication and public health notification
Secondary cellulitis, abscess or signs of systemic sepsis
Involvement of the eye, sinuses or central structures threatening deep spread
Infestation in a neglected, debilitated or cognitively impaired patient
reference.prognosis: Furuncular myiasis is generally benign and resolves completely once the larva is removed, whereas wound and cavity myiasis, especially screwworm, can cause serious tissue destruction and requires urgent intervention; secondary infection is the main complication.
pitfalls: Rupturing or fragmenting the larva during extraction, leaving parts that provoke a foreign-body reaction
Misdiagnosing furuncular myiasis as a simple boil and incising without recognising the larva
Underestimating aggressive wound or cavity myiasis and its capacity for deep destruction
Neglecting tetanus prophylaxis and secondary infection management
Failing to notify authorities for obligate parasites such as screwworm where reportable
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
